children.author: snackbroken
children.text: Funnily enough, Youtube recently changed how they count views to be more in line with its competitors, so now they do count views as soon as the video starts playing.

You can consider adding in a small amount of js that tracks if a person actually engages with the content before "counting" their view. Eg, did they stay on the page for more than 15 seconds.

Youtube wont count a view until you watch for some percentage of the video. Maybe consider something similar.

I know you can't be super specific because you'd just be enabling the companies who get around this (who, funnily, I also index on The Consensus), but I have spent a few rounds on this over the months and haven't yet been able to cut them out.

Some of the things that seemed like they'd cut out lazier bots/scripters involved browser fingerprinting that I didn't want to yet have to deal with disclosures or approval for. But also even some of these browser fingerprinting things were disable-able via flags when you start up Chrome or whatever.

I think what would work overall is to track all requests for a pattern of page access and start blocking other systems that are part of that pattern. But that also wouldn't account for like... landing on the front page of HN, which happens not infrequently.

All of this is aside from per-IP or per-user proof of work. Whenever someone lands on a more expensive page I make the browser do proof of work and store it in a cookie, unique to the IP or user. (Signed in users don't have to do proof of work). This is a perfect solution except for the IP rotation I'm talking about above.

edit: ah also, I don't do SSL termination so can't spot the SSL configuration. But Cloudflare does. And all of this is even after Cloudflare paid bot traffic systems are in place.

edit 2:

> tiny percentage of bots will still get through but the load becomes much more manageable.

The load is not the problem. It's only at most a few bot hits per second. I'm just having trouble removing bot attribution from view counts.

Bots give all the information required to block or rate limit them including those that try to look like a real browser (some things they just can't hide, even residential proxies via behavior.). Ask the LLM how to change your log format to gather all the fields your web server can see. Share the resulting updated logs with your favorite LLM. Ask it for generalized rules to block the bots whilst permitting real browsers. A tiny percentage of bots will still get through but the load becomes much more manageable. Tell your LLM you also wish to spot fake chrome via CH and bots via ssl curves. No need for JA3. Nginx can expose the important aspects of GREASE.

children.author: EvanAnderson
children.text:
I mind a public access website for a government entity and this is exactly the pattern I see. US residential IPs make a couple of requests then never come back.

The bots may have layer 7 signatures that make them "easy" to block, but I'm dealing with COTS software with no ability to make changes to the stack. Even if I could by the time they're blocked the work is done and they're never coming back anyway.

I don't think I'm seeing the LLM bots in the scraping on this particular site. This site's data is highly sought-after by data brokers, legal services advertising, debt collectors, etc. I tend to think I'm seeing homespun scrapers. This site has been up for 20+ years and the scrapers seem to be well-adapted to using the HTML as an ad-hoc API for the data. The difference in the last few years has been the availability of vast numbers of residential proxies to mask the traffic.

I get tens of thousands of IPs making 1 or 2 requests against pages on The Consensus (job search, code viewing, etc.). They're not super expensive pages. But I don't want to deal with the bot traffic (mostly because it messes up view counts I use to sell sponsorships). But then if I require an account (even a free one), valid readership is also going to drop with the new friction.

I could build something more complex to discover the patterns, or use Turnstile maybe. I'm not really sure at the moment.

You're welcome.

Before pushing such things to production consider first testing in dev/qa then staging or some canary environment. I use those IP's to determine who gets into a moderator review queue so worst case it just makes more work for me. Consider using those in conjunction with whatever rate limiting capabilities your web server provides first so it is not a hard block in the unlikely event a real customer shows up on one of them.
Thanks. I will definitely explore these in production.

FireHol [1] and lists_vpn [2] are useful for nginx geo files. Be sure to use iprange [3] to aggregate cidr ranges, IP's or lists get big fast The IP ranges can be used in conjunction with rate limiting and/or firewall ipsets and/or blackhole routing tables depending on what type of abuse your site is receiving.

LLM's can help you implement iprange into IP list building scripts to keep the lists smaller and more efficient.

[1] - https://github.com/firehol/blocklist-ipsets/

[2] - https://github.com/X4BNet/lists_vpn

[3] - https://github.com/firehol/iprange

> That said there are some good IP lists that can be used in blackhole routing tables, nginx geo tables, etc...

I focus on content on our site so blocking part of internet with wordfence was brute but as life has only few thousands of weeks, it was the least I wanted to think about :).

Would you mind to share a source of good IP lists pls?

eventually throttled by OAI or Anthropic themselves

Indeed, they use an edge SSL Bump proxy that is already bandwidth limited and has to speak real HTTPS.

I do not focus too much on IP addresses but rather the behavior that they can not hide. LLM's can help you spot this behavior. Good LLM vs. Bad LLM. Gemini knows a few tricks but you have to coax it out of them. It seems to not want to overload people with information. That said there are some good IP lists that can be used in blackhole routing tables, nginx geo tables, etc...

LLM bots make only a part of traffic and really easy to set up (and I think this will eventually throttled by OAI or Anthropic themselves).

But there are bad actors - bots that try every possible urls and traversals and cross scripting and so on… I see it in our access logs. This cannot be solved otherwise than some greylisting/blacklisting on ISP level. E.g. this is so huge that we have started to block all Chinese inbound traffic. I am sorry for that because Deepseek and other good actors are probably blocked as well but IP rotation made it impossible to filter bad ones only… (and I suppose that DS uses EU or US addresses as well so they shouldn’t be blocked in full).

children.text:
Not a hope. Anthropic have proven that when they admitted to indisputable breaches of the CFAA twice.

(1) They admitted its Claude models had breached the systems of three companies since April; including Huggingface.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-30/anthropic...

(2) They secured unauthorised access to a U.S. state government website hosting election-related data, pulling aggregate vote-count statistics from a gated government dashboard. The state government itself confirmed the access was entirely unauthorised.

https://seekingalpha.com/news/4657023-anthropics-claude-bypa...

If a human security researcher had deployed an agent that behaved this way, it would constitute a textbook felony under the CFAA for accessing those systems without authorisation.

Unfortunately different rules apply when you have the power to buy off Congress and the Appeals Courts.

Most recently a US appeals court ruled on 5 August that Amazon was unlikely to succeed on a claim that Perplexity's AI agents violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by covertly accessing private Amazon customer accounts.

https://www.rte.ie/news/technology/2026/0807/1586941-artific...

I was not aware of that (terrible) court decision. Wow.

I suppose this is one of those laws that doesn't apply if an individual is a victim? I have a email box that sometimes fills with spam and rejects legitimate email. Can I get the corporations that filled it up to be charged with felonies?

The problem is unintentional DOS due to traffic can constitute a felony under the CFAA; the case in question being Pulte Homes, Inc. v. Laborers' International Union 2011.

After Pulte fired an employee represented by the union, LIUNA urged members to call and send email to the company, expressing their opinions. As a result of the increased traffic, the company's email system crashed. The Sixth Circuit ruled that the LIUNA's instruction to call and email "intentionally caused damage," reversing the lower court's decision.

Now thankfully we have Sandvig v. Barr, 2020 where the DC Federal Court ruled that the CFAA does not criminalize the violation of a website's terms of service, but imo all bets are off in terms of interpretation of the law in the wild west of AI.

But, per groups of queries, the worst they've seen is 11 thousand, and that's across many libraries. So, some tiny fraction of their users amplified their traffic by 11,000x by using a misconfigured LLM. I've done that a few times without LLMs (who hasn't passed --recursive to wget without remembering the -np?)

Also, if they just turned off all the user-hostile crap, they'd probably get at least 1000x back on their serving costs. How much does it cost to serve a login gate, captcha and rejection screen vs. a ~1MB static file?. What about the human cost where actual users cannot get access to the data they should have access to?

Just now, I ran a Kagi search. Its LLM summarized some page on the internet, but when I went to check the reference, I got a "sorry, humans only" access denied error message. I guess it's good that I could ask the LLM to quote the document verbatim for me in a follow up message, but what fresh hell is this? (Also, the error message screen was clearly longer than the document I'd requested.)

It's 11 THOUSAND searches ON JUST THAT ONE TOPIC in one day when they are used to seeing less than 11 THOUSAND searches in one day TOTAL. None of these systems were built for this type of traffic. The total traffic from these crawlers is many times more than just 11,000. It's more like 11,000 searches on 100,000 topics.

11 THOUSAND searches in one day? What's the problem?

If anything, libraries should be becoming more AI friendly, not less. Instead, we get this sort of bullshit from the ACM:

https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3832783.3834511

It's a canonical DOI on what was a download server. It says exactly which file is being requested. (I chose a random recent one.) At the very most, they should serve a static page with a bibtex entry, and a few other metadata fields, and a link to the PDF and whatever other formats are available.

Instead, we get piles of captchas, login-gate spam about how they're "open access" now and have some initiative to be LLM friendly.

Getting back to the problem of people doing stuff that requires access to library materials: What sort of server-side cost multiplier do you suppose this ACM page has vs. just serving a few S3-compatible URLs that point to a few mirrors? (Or, got forbid, Anna's Archive / libgen, since ACM is open access, and those sites would be doing nothing wrong by mirroring ACM content.)
